title: Comparison and logical operators; short-circuit evaluation
learningObjectives: Use relational operators to compare arithmetic values.
Combine conditions with logical AND, OR and NOT.
Use short-circuiting to guard operations that require a prior condition.
Distinguish logical operators from bitwise operators and avoid chained-comparison mistakes.

understand.concept: Relational operators compare values and produce an int result of 0 or 1. Logical operators &&, || and ! combine or negate conditions and also produce 0 or 1. The && and || operators short-circuit: the right operand is evaluated only when needed. This sequencing can protect an operation, such as dereferencing a pointer only after checking it, when the left condition establishes the required precondition.
understand.whyItMatters: Understanding Comparison and logical operators; short-circuit evaluation helps you reason about program behaviour instead of memorizing syntax. It is useful in exams, debugging and building reliable C applications.
understand.analogy: Treat the concept as a tool with a precise contract: it has valid inputs, defined operations and observable results.
understand.analogyLimit: An analogy is only an aid; the C standard and the relevant function specifications determine actual behaviour.

explain.narrative:
## 1. Relational comparisons

C provides `<`, `<=`, `>`, `>=`, `==` and `!=`. They compare values after the applicable conversions and produce an int value of 0 or 1.

## 2. Logical operators

`A && B` is true only when both conditions are true. `A || B` is true when at least one condition is true. `!A` negates the truth value of A. In C, zero is false and nonzero is true.

## 3. Short-circuit evaluation

For `A && B`, B is evaluated only if A is true. For `A || B`, B is evaluated only if A is false. This is useful for checks such as `ptr != NULL && *ptr > 0`, because the dereference is skipped when ptr is null.

## 4. Logical is not bitwise

`&&` and `||` operate on truth conditions and short-circuit. `&` and `|` operate bit by bit on integer operands and evaluate both operands.

## 5. Avoid chained comparisons

An expression such as `0 < x < 10` does not test whether x is between zero and ten. It compares `0 < x` first, then compares that 0-or-1 result with 10. Write `x > 0 && x < 10` instead.

questions.prompt: What value does a relational expression produce in C?
questions.explanation: Relational operators produce an int result representing false or true.

questions.prompt: When is the right operand of A && B evaluated?
questions.explanation: Logical AND short-circuits when the left operand is false.

questions.prompt: Which expression safely checks ptr before dereferencing it?
questions.explanation: The left operand is evaluated first and a null pointer prevents evaluation of the dereference.

questions.prompt: What is wrong with `0 < x < 10` as a range test?
options: It compares the result of 0 < x with 10 rather than testing both bounds
It is always a syntax error
questions.answer: It compares the result of 0 < x with 10 rather than testing both bounds
questions.explanation: Use two relational expressions joined by &&.

questions.prompt: Which pair is logical rather than bitwise?
questions.explanation: The doubled operators are logical and short-circuiting.
